leaders.name: Alexander
leaders.polity: Kingdom of Macedon and the empire it conquered

personality.temperament: Alexander could not stay still. He slept little, drank hard, wept at the deaths of friends and killed one of them in a quarrel. He led from the front and carried the wounds to prove it. Plutarch records a man who wanted glory more than land and who asked his tutor, Aristotle, for more worlds. His soldiers followed him past the edge of every map they knew.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Short Life of Glory, rewards leaders at war and scorns those at peace; the historical Alexander fought for eleven of his thirteen years as king.

leaders.bio_codex: Alexander came to the throne of Macedon at twenty, in 336 BCE, after his father Philip was murdered at a wedding. Within two years he had burned Thebes and crossed into Asia with forty thousand men. At the Granicus, at Issus and at Gaugamela he broke the armies of Darius III, and by 331 the Persian Empire was his. He took Egypt and was named pharaoh, founded Alexandria, burned Persepolis, and marched east through Bactria into the Punjab, where his army refused to go further. He turned back along the desert coast and died in Babylon in June 323 BCE, aged thirty-two, of a fever or a poison; the sources disagree. He left no settled heir. His generals divided the world he had taken, and the Greek language, Greek cities and Greek gods settled in it for three centuries after him. Cities fell to him by the hundred; the people in them were sold or spared at his mood.
leaders.legacy: He conquered the known world in eleven years and left it to be fought over for forty.

quote.text: There is nothing impossible to him who will try.
quote.source: Attributed to Alexander; recorded in later collections, not in a contemporary source

leaders.name: Amanitore

personality.temperament: The record of Amanitore is in stone, not in words. Her name stands beside Natakamani's on temples at Naqa, Amun's great hall at Meroë and the restored sanctuary at Jebel Barkal. The Lion Temple shows her striding, broad-shouldered, a sword raised over bound captives. The kandakes of Kush ruled as warriors and builders, and she was shown as both. Rome's writers noted queens in Meroë and did not name her.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, City Planner, favours leaders who build districts; the historical Amanitore's reign is the most productive building period in Meroitic history.

leaders.bio_codex: Amanitore ruled the Kingdom of Kush from Meroë, on the Nile between the fifth and sixth cataracts, in the first half of the first century CE. She held the title kandake, queen, and governed alongside Natakamani, who may have been her husband or her son; the inscriptions name them together and give her equal size and equal regalia. Their reign was the last great age of Meroitic building. They restored the temple of Amun at Meroë, built the Lion Temple and the Amun temple at Naqa, repaired Jebel Barkal and raised reservoirs along the river. Kush had treated with Augustus a generation earlier and now traded with Rome in gold, ivory and iron. Her pyramid stands at Meroë in the northern cemetery, steeper and smaller than Egypt's, and robbed long before archaeologists reached it. The Meroitic script on her monuments has still not been read in full.
leaders.legacy: She built more of Kush than any ruler before or after her, and her name is on all of it.

leaders.name: Ambiorix
leaders.polity: Eburones, a Belgic tribe of Gaul

personality.temperament: Everything known of Ambiorix comes from the man who hunted him. Caesar presents him as a talker who could turn a Roman officer's trust into a trap, and a fighter who knew when to leave a field. He parleyed, lied, ambushed, and vanished into the forest with four horsemen when the legions came for him. The Eburones were destroyed for his sake; he was never caught.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Scourge of Rome, dislikes leaders who build large armies; the historical Ambiorix was the Belgic king who nearly broke Caesar's hold on Gaul.

leaders.bio_codex: Ambiorix ruled half the Eburones, a Belgic people between the Meuse and the Rhine, under Caesar's occupation of Gaul. In the winter of 54 BCE, with a Roman legion and five cohorts quartered on his land, he persuaded their commanders, Sabinus and Cotta, that a general rising was coming and that he would see them safely to another camp. He ambushed the column in a valley and destroyed it, the heaviest Roman loss of the whole war. He then raised the Nervii and Aduatuci and besieged Quintus Cicero's camp until Caesar himself broke the siege. In 53 BCE Caesar invited every tribe in Gaul to plunder the Eburones and marched through their country with fire. Ambiorix escaped across the Rhine with a few riders, and the record ends there. Nineteenth-century Belgium made him a national hero and put his statue in Tongeren, the Roman town that replaced his people.
leaders.legacy: He destroyed a legion by talking to it, and the Romans erased his nation to find him.

leaders.name: Bà Triệu

dates.historicity: historical in Vietnamese tradition; Chinese sources are thin

leaders.polity: Jiuzhen (Cửu Chân) under the Chinese Wu dynasty, in what became Vietnam
titles: Nhụy Kiều Tướng quân (the Lady General Clad in Golden Robe)

personality.temperament: The Vietnamese tradition gives her a sentence that outlived her: that she would ride the storm, tread the waves, cut the whale from the eastern sea, sweep the frontier, and never bend her back to be a man's concubine. Chinese chroniclers called her a bandit and noted her height and her elephant. She refused marriage, refused her brother's caution and refused surrender.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Defender of the Homeland, likes leaders who hold their own lands and dislikes those who take cities from her; she fought one war, against an occupier.

leaders.bio_codex: Triệu Thị Trinh was born in 225 CE in the district of Cửu Chân, in the Thanh Hóa country south of the Red River, under the rule of the Chinese state of Wu. Tradition says she killed a sister-in-law who abused her, went into the mountains, and gathered a thousand followers before she was twenty. In 248 she led a rising against the Wu governor, riding to battle on an elephant in yellow robes with a sword in each hand, and took the fortified towns of the district. Wu sent the general Lu Yin with eight thousand men. After several months of fighting her force broke, and she withdrew to Mount Tùng and died there, by her own hand according to the Vietnamese accounts. She was twenty-three. Later kings built her a temple and granted her posthumous titles, and her name was taken by Vietnamese nationalists for a thousand years of risings that came after.
leaders.legacy: She rose at twenty-three against the empire next door and set the pattern for every Vietnamese rising that followed.

quote.text: I want to ride the storm, tread the dangerous waves, win back the fatherland and destroy the yoke of slavery.
quote.source: Attributed in Vietnamese tradition; recorded in later chronicles, not in a contemporary source

leaders.name: Basil II

personality.temperament: Psellos, who knew men who had served him, described an emperor who gave up wine, women, jewels and conversation, slept on the ground with his soldiers, and spoke in short sentences in a soldier's voice. He trusted no aristocrat after two of them tried to take his throne, and he ruled through eunuchs and the army. He laughed rarely. He campaigned every year of his adult life.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Porphyrogénnētos, respects leaders with strong cavalry and distrusts those who neglect it; Basil's empire was built on the armoured horse.

leaders.bio_codex: Basil was born in the purple chamber of the palace in 958 and crowned co-emperor at two. He did not rule until 976, and for the first thirteen years of his reign the generals Skleros and Phokas each rose against him; he broke the second at Abydos in 989 with six thousand Varangians sent by Vladimir of Kiev, to whom he gave his sister in marriage and the Orthodox faith. He then turned on Bulgaria and fought it for thirty years. At Kleidion in 1014 he took fourteen thousand prisoners and, by the chroniclers' account, blinded ninety-nine of every hundred and sent them home led by the hundredth; Tsar Samuel died at the sight. Bulgaria fell in 1018 and the Danube was Rome's frontier again. He annexed Armenian lands, held Syria against the Fatimids, and filled a treasury that his heirs emptied in a generation. He never married and died in 1025 planning an expedition to Sicily.
leaders.legacy: He ruled for forty-nine years, restored the Danube frontier, and left an empire at its height to heirs who could not hold it.

leaders.name: Catherine de Medici

dates.display: Queen consort 1547 to 1559; regent and queen mother to 1589

personality.temperament: She was orphaned at three weeks, held hostage in a convent during the siege of Florence, and married at fourteen to a prince who preferred his mistress for twenty-five years. She waited. When her husband died she governed through three sons, balancing Catholic and Huguenot factions that each wanted the other dead, and she spent what the treasury did not have on festivals, ballets and palaces. Her enemies made her a poisoner; the record makes her a survivor.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Black Queen, favours leaders with strong intelligence networks and distrusts those who keep none; she ran the most elaborate court of spies in Europe.

leaders.bio_codex: Caterina de' Medici was born in Florence in 1519, the last legitimate heir of the elder Medici line, and was married at fourteen to Henri, second son of Francis I of France, in a bargain between the French crown and her uncle Pope Clement VII. She bore ten children after a decade of barrenness. Henri II died in a tournament in 1559 and she governed for three sons in succession, Francis II, Charles IX and Henri III, through the Wars of Religion. She tried toleration first, at Saint-Germain in 1562, and failed. In August 1572, days after her daughter's wedding to the Protestant Henri of Navarre, Paris murdered thousands of Huguenots in the Saint Bartholomew's Day massacre; how far she ordered it is still argued, and she did not stop it. She built the Tuileries, bought Chenonceau, commissioned Nostradamus and Ronsard, and died in January 1589 eight months before her last son was stabbed to death.
leaders.legacy: She held the French crown together through thirty years of civil war and three weak kings, at a price Paris still remembers.

leaders.name: Chandragupta

personality.temperament: Greek sources knew him as Sandrokottos, a young man who had seen Alexander's camp and judged that an empire could be taken. Indian tradition gives him a teacher, Chanakya, whose treatise on statecraft counsels spies, bribes and surprise. He took the throne by force, held it with a vast army and a vaster bureaucracy, and at the end, the Jain accounts say, gave it up and starved himself to death as a monk.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Boundless Ambition, pushes him to expand into any neighbour's land; the historical Chandragupta took the whole of northern India in twenty years.

leaders.bio_codex: Chandragupta rose from obscure origins in the Magadha country in the years after Alexander's withdrawal from the Indus. Around 321 BCE, guided by the Brahmin strategist Chanakya, he overthrew the Nanda dynasty and took Pataliputra on the Ganges. He then pushed west into the Punjab, drove out the Macedonian garrisons, and in 305 met Seleucus I, Alexander's successor in Asia, in war. The peace that followed gave Chandragupta the provinces of the Hindu Kush and gave Seleucus five hundred war elephants and a marriage alliance. Seleucus's envoy Megasthenes lived at his court and wrote of a city nine miles long, an army of six hundred thousand, and a king who feared assassination enough to sleep in a different room each night. His empire ran from Afghanistan to Bengal. Late in life he abdicated for his son Bindusara, followed the Jain teacher Bhadrabahu south to Shravanabelagola, and died there by ritual fast.
leaders.legacy: He founded the first empire to hold most of India and gave it up to die as a monk.

leaders.name: Cleopatra

personality.temperament: Plutarch said her beauty was not remarkable but her voice and conversation were, and that she spoke Egyptian, which no Ptolemy before her had bothered to learn, along with Greek, Ethiopian, Hebrew, Arabic, Syriac, Median and Parthian. She chose her allies among the most powerful men alive and bore their children. When the last alliance failed she chose her own death over a Roman triumph.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Queen of the Nile, likes leaders with strong militaries and dislikes weak ones; she allied with Caesar and Antony because each was the strongest man in Rome.

leaders.bio_codex: Cleopatra VII Philopator was born in 69 BCE, the daughter of Ptolemy XII, in a Greek dynasty that had ruled Egypt since Alexander's general took it. She became queen in 51 BCE beside her brother, lost a civil war to him, and in 48 had herself carried into Caesar's quarters in Alexandria rolled in a carpet or a bedroll; the brother drowned in the Nile and she ruled. She bore Caesar a son, Caesarion, and lived in Rome until Caesar was killed. In 41 she met Mark Antony at Tarsus, sailing up the Cydnus in a gilded barge, and over ten years bore him three children and bound Egypt's treasury to his half of the Roman world. Octavian defeated them at Actium in 31 BCE. Antony fell on his sword; Cleopatra, taken in her mausoleum, died in August 30 BCE, by an asp in the tradition and by poison in all likelihood. Egypt became a Roman province. She was the last pharaoh.
leaders.legacy: She was the last ruler of independent Egypt, and she chose the manner of its ending.

leaders.name: Cyrus
titles: King of the Four Corners of the World

personality.temperament: The Greeks, who had every reason to hate Persia, admired him. Xenophon made him the model of a just king and Herodotus gave him a childhood out of legend. The clay cylinder he left in Babylon speaks of restoring temples and sending exiles home, and the Hebrew prophets called him anointed. He moved faster than his enemies expected and treated the conquered as subjects rather than spoil.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Opportunist, likes leaders who declare surprise wars and dislikes those who never do; Cyrus took Lydia by marching in winter when Croesus had sent his army home.

leaders.bio_codex: Cyrus became king of the Persians at Anshan around 559 BCE, a vassal of the Medes, and within a decade had overthrown his overlord Astyages and taken Ecbatana. In 547 or 546 he marched on Lydia, fought Croesus to a draw at Pteria, and then followed him home to Sardis in the off-season and took the city. The Greek cities of Ionia fell to his generals. In 539 he entered Babylon, the sources say without a battle, after the Euphrates was diverted or the garrison opened the gates. He let the Jews return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple, kept the Babylonian gods in their shrines and himself in the local titles, and governed through satraps and roads. He died in 530 BCE campaigning in Central Asia against the Massagetae; Herodotus says Queen Tomyris had his head put in a skin of blood. His tomb at Pasargadae is a plain stone house on six steps, and Alexander, who found it looted, had it restored.
leaders.legacy: He built the largest empire the world had seen and governed it by leaving its peoples their gods.

leaders.name: Dido

dates.display: fl. c. 814 BCE (traditional founding of Carthage)
dates.historicity: legendary; Carthage's founding is historical, its founder is tradition

leaders.polity: Carthage, a Phoenician colony of Tyre

personality.temperament: The tradition remembers a woman who outwitted a brother, a landlord and a god. She fled Tyre with her husband's treasure and a company of nobles, asked the Libyan king for as much land as an ox-hide would cover, and cut the hide into a thread that enclosed a hill. Virgil gave her a Trojan lover and a funeral pyre; the Carthaginian version, lost with the city, made her die rather than marry a Libyan king.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Sicilian Wars, likes leaders who settle away from her and dislikes those who settle near her coast; the historical Carthage fought Greece for Sicily for three centuries.

leaders.bio_codex: Elissa, called Dido, was by tradition a princess of Tyre, sister of King Pygmalion, who murdered her husband the priest Acerbas for his gold. She took the gold and a company of followers, sailed west by way of Cyprus, and landed on the coast of Libya near the modern city of Tunis. There she bought from the Berber king Iarbas the land an ox-hide could cover and, cutting it into strips, enclosed the hill called Byrsa, the hide. The city founded there, Qart-hadasht, the new city, grew into Carthage, the greatest trading power of the western Mediterranean, with harbours, a navy, and colonies from Spain to Sicily. The founding date given by ancient writers is 814 BCE, and archaeology finds Phoenician settlement on the site by the late ninth century. Dido herself has left no inscription, no coin and no tomb. Timaeus told her story first; Virgil gave her to Aeneas; Carthage, which kept its own account, was burned by Rome in 146 BCE.
leaders.legacy: She founded the city that fought Rome for the Mediterranean, and Rome's poet gave her the only story of her that survives.

leaders.name: Eleanor of Aquitaine

dates.display: Duchess of Aquitaine 1137 to 1204; Queen of France 1137 to 1152; Queen of England 1154 to 1189

leaders.polity: Duchy of Aquitaine; Kingdom of France; Kingdom of England (Angevin Empire)

personality.temperament: She outlived two husbands, both kings, and eight of her ten children. She went on crusade with the first, divorced him, married the second ten weeks later, rebelled against him with their sons and spent sixteen years in his custody. Freed at seventy, she rode across Europe to ransom one son and to fetch a bride for another. The troubadours sang in her court and the chroniclers, mostly clerics, disapproved of her in detail.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Angevin Empire, likes leaders with high loyalty and dislikes those whose cities waver; her own lands followed her from one crown to the other.

leaders.bio_codex: Eleanor inherited Aquitaine, a third of France, at fifteen on her father's death in 1137 and was married within months to Louis VII of France. She went with him on the Second Crusade, quarrelled with him at Antioch, and had the marriage annulled in 1152 on grounds of kinship. Eight weeks later she married Henry Plantagenet, eleven years younger, who in 1154 became Henry II of England. Her dowry made him lord of more of France than the French king. She bore him eight children, including Richard the Lionheart and John, and in 1173 backed her sons' revolt against him; he kept her confined until his death in 1189. As queen mother she governed England during Richard's crusade, raised his ransom from the Emperor, and at eighty crossed the Pyrenees to bring her granddaughter Blanche to marry the heir of France. She died at Fontevraud in 1204 and lies there in effigy, reading a book.
leaders.legacy: She carried a third of France from one crown to the other and outlasted every man who tried to rule her.

leaders.name: Frederick Barbarossa

personality.temperament: Red-bearded, broad, courteous in speech and relentless in purpose, he spent his reign trying to make the empire a fact rather than a title. He crossed the Alps six times to make the cities of Lombardy obey and burned Milan when they would not. He treated with popes and made antipopes. He died at nearly seventy in a river in Anatolia, in armour, on his way to Jerusalem; the legend has him asleep under a mountain waiting to come back.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Iron Crown, dislikes leaders who ally with or hold city-states he wants; he spent thirty years fighting the free communes of Italy.

leaders.bio_codex: Frederick of Hohenstaufen, duke of Swabia, was elected king of Germany in 1152 as a compromise between the Welf and Staufen factions that had torn the kingdom. Pope Adrian IV crowned him emperor in Rome in 1155. He issued the Roncaglia decrees in 1158 claiming the regalian rights of the Lombard cities, and the cities refused him; he razed Milan in 1162, lost his army to malaria outside Rome in 1167, and was beaten by the Lombard League at Legnano in 1176. He made peace at Constance in 1183, keeping the title and conceding the substance. In Germany he broke the power of Henry the Lion, settled the eastern marches, and married his son to the heiress of Sicily. In 1189 he took the Third Crusade east with the largest army of the three. On 10 June 1190 he drowned crossing the Saleph river in Cilicia, and his army dissolved.
leaders.legacy: He spent thirty-eight years making the Holy Roman Empire mean what its name said, and drowned on the way to Jerusalem.

leaders.name: Gandhi

dates.display: led the Indian independence movement 1915 to 1947

leaders.polity: British India; the Indian independence movement
titles: Leader of the Indian National Congress

personality.temperament: He called his autobiography the story of his experiments with truth, and he ran the experiments on himself: diet, celibacy, silence, fasting to the edge of death to stop a riot. He was a lawyer who dressed as a peasant, a Hindu who read the Sermon on the Mount, and a man who answered an empire's police with a march to the sea to make salt. He was shot by a Hindu who thought him too soft on Muslims.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Peacekeeper, likes leaders at peace and refuses to forgive warmongers; the historical Gandhi built a national movement on non-violence.

leaders.bio_codex: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born in Porbandar in 1869, trained as a barrister in London, and spent twenty-one years in South Africa, where he was thrown off a train for his colour and began the campaigns of civil disobedience he named satyagraha. He returned to India in 1915. He led the non-cooperation movement of 1920, the Salt March of 1930, walking 240 miles to the sea to break the British monopoly, and the Quit India campaign of 1942, and he spent more than six years of his life in prison for them. He worked for the untouchables, for village industry and for Hindu-Muslim unity, and he fasted against the violence of partition in 1947 while the country he had freed divided itself in blood. On 30 January 1948 Nathuram Godse shot him three times at a prayer meeting in Delhi. He held no office and commanded no army. Independent India has his face on every banknote.
leaders.legacy: He freed a nation without an army and was killed by one of his own for the peace he kept.

quote.text: The weak can never forgive. Forgiveness is the attribute of the strong.

leaders.name: Genghis Khan

personality.temperament: Temüjin was abandoned by his clan as a boy, enslaved, and hunted; he killed his half-brother over a fish. As khan he rewarded loyalty above birth, promoted a herdsman to general and a captured enemy archer to the head of his army, and made treachery to any master, even his enemy, a capital crime. He asked Taoist sages about immortality and let every faith pray for him. He emptied cities that resisted.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Horse Lord, likes leaders with strong cavalry and resents those who field it against him; the Mongol army was horse, bow and nothing else.

leaders.bio_codex: Temüjin was born on the Onon river around 1162 to a minor chieftain who was poisoned when the boy was nine. He spent his youth hunted, captured and freed, and built a following from the dispossessed. By 1206 he had defeated or absorbed every tribe on the steppe and was proclaimed Chinggis Khan at a great assembly. He reorganised the Mongols into decimal units with no regard to clan, issued a written law, and turned outward. He broke the Western Xia, took Beijing from the Jin in 1215, and when the Khwarazmian shah murdered his envoys in 1219 he destroyed that empire in three years; Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv and Nishapur were depopulated. His generals rode around the Caspian and beat the Russian princes on the Kalka. He died in August 1227 on campaign against Xia, from a fall or a wound, and was buried in secret. His sons and grandsons ruled from Korea to Hungary.
leaders.legacy: He took a scattered people and made them the largest land empire in history, and the cities that refused him were erased.

leaders.name: Gilgamesh

dates.historicity: legendary; possibly a historical king of Uruk, later deified

titles: Hero of the Epic of Gilgamesh

personality.temperament: The epic opens with a king too strong for his city, who wears out its young men and takes its brides, until the gods make him an equal, Enkidu, out of clay. The two fight, embrace, and go to kill the guardian of the cedar forest together. When Enkidu dies, Gilgamesh wanders the earth in a lion skin looking for a way not to. He comes home without one and looks at his walls.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Ally of Enkidu, seeks long alliances and defends his friends; the epic's whole second half is grief for one.

leaders.bio_codex: Gilgamesh appears in the Sumerian King List as the fifth king of the first dynasty of Uruk, reigning 126 years, and in inscriptions of later kings who claimed him as a brother or a god. If he lived, it was around 2700 BCE, in the city on the Euphrates whose walls he is credited with building, nine kilometres of baked brick around what was then the largest settlement in the world. The poems about him were written in Sumerian by 2100 BCE and gathered into the Akkadian Epic of Gilgamesh by the end of the second millennium; the standard version, twelve tablets, was found in the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh in 1853. It tells of his friendship with Enkidu, the killing of Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven, Enkidu's death, the journey to Utnapishtim who survived the flood, and the return to Uruk with nothing but the knowledge that the walls would outlast him. The walls are still there, a mound in the desert called Warka.
leaders.legacy: He is the first hero whose name is written down, and his story is the oldest one still read.

leaders.name: Gitarja

personality.temperament: The Javanese chronicles call her Tribhuwana, ruler of the three worlds, and Gitarja is the childhood name the Pararaton preserves. She took the throne when her brother died without a son, put down a rebellion in person, and appointed as chief minister Gajah Mada, who swore an oath not to taste spice until the archipelago was hers. She let him keep it. She is shown in temple statuary as the goddess Parvati.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Exalted Goddess of the Three Worlds, likes leaders who hold faith and dislikes those with none; Majapahit's queen was carved as a goddess in her own lifetime.

leaders.bio_codex: Dyah Gitarja was the daughter of Raden Wijaya, founder of Majapahit, and of Gayatri Rajapatni, a princess of the older kingdom of Singhasari. When her half-brother Jayanegara was murdered in 1328 the succession passed through her mother, who had become a Buddhist nun, and Gitarja ruled in her name under the title Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi. In 1331 she led the army herself against the rebellion of Sadeng and Keta in eastern Java. She raised Gajah Mada to mahapatih, chief minister, in 1334, and under his Palapa oath Majapahit took Bali in 1343 and sent fleets to Sumatra, Borneo and the Malay coast. She abdicated in 1350 when her mother died and the regency ended, and her son Hayam Wuruk reigned over the empire at its height. She lived on at court for two decades more. Her memorial statue at Candi Rimbi shows her as Parvati with four arms.
leaders.legacy: She took Majapahit from a murdered brother and handed her son the largest sea empire in Southeast Asian history.
