leaders.name: Gorgo

dates.display: Queen consort of Sparta c. 490 to 480 BCE
dates.historicity: historical; known through Herodotus and Plutarch

personality.temperament: Herodotus tells of her at eight or nine warning her father not to be bribed by a Milesian with a case for war; the king sent the man away. When a blank wax tablet came to Sparta she was the one who guessed the message was under the wax. Asked by an Athenian woman why Spartan women alone ruled their men, Plutarch has her say, because we alone give birth to men. She sent Leonidas to Thermopylae with instructions to marry a good man and bear good children.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, With Your Shield or On It, respects leaders who never give up cities and despises those who do; her husband's three hundred did not retreat.

leaders.bio_codex: Gorgo was the only child of Cleomenes I, king of Sparta of the Agiad line, and was born around 518 BCE. She married her uncle Leonidas, who succeeded to the throne in about 490 after Cleomenes died, mad or murdered, in prison. Herodotus, who wrote within living memory, gives her two of the few recorded sayings of any Spartan woman and credits her with reading the secret message from Demaratus that warned Greece of Xerxes' invasion. In 480 Leonidas marched north with three hundred Spartans and died at Thermopylae holding the pass; their son Pleistarchus was a child, and Gorgo's brother-in-law Cleombrotus and then her nephew Pausanias held the regency. Her later life is unrecorded. Sparta kept no histories of its own, and what survives of Gorgo is what Athenians and a Boeotian chose to remember: a girl who was listened to, and a queen who told the truth in one sentence.
leaders.legacy: She is the one Spartan woman whose words the Greeks wrote down, and they were all about not yielding.

quote.text: Because we are the only women who give birth to men.
quote.source: Plutarch, Sayings of Spartan Women, Gorgo 5

leaders.name: Hammurabi

dates.display: r. c. 1792 to c. 1750 BCE (middle chronology)

personality.temperament: His letters survive by the hundred, written to governors about canals, late taxes, a stolen ox and a bribed judge. He waited thirty years before making war on his rivals and then took them one by one. The stele of his laws shows him standing before the sun god, receiving the rod and ring of justice, and its prologue says he was called to make justice visible in the land so that the strong should not oppress the weak.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Cradle of Civilization, likes leaders who build and run many district types and dislikes those who build few; his laws governed every trade in Babylon.

leaders.bio_codex: Hammurabi inherited Babylon in about 1792 BCE as one of a dozen Amorite kingdoms on the rivers of Mesopotamia, hemmed by Larsa, Eshnunna, Mari and Assyria. For three decades he dug canals, built walls and kept treaties. Then, in a span of about ten years from 1763, he beat Elam and Larsa, took Eshnunna, destroyed Mari, which had been his ally, and made Babylon the capital of all of Sumer and Akkad. His code of 282 laws, cut into a two-metre stele of black diorite near the end of his reign, set prices, wages, divorce terms, the liability of builders whose houses fell, and the lex talionis, an eye for an eye between equals and silver between unequals. The stele was carried off to Susa by the Elamites six centuries later and found there in 1901. His empire shrank under his son and was gone within a century and a half; the laws were copied in schools for a thousand years.
leaders.legacy: He wrote the oldest long code of law that survives and set it where everyone could read it.

leaders.name: Harald Hardrada

personality.temperament: He fought his first battle at fifteen and lost it. He fled to Kiev, then to Constantinople, where he led the emperor's Varangian axemen in Sicily, Bulgaria and the Holy Land, came home with a ship's hold of gold, and bought half a kingdom with it. He composed poetry, blinded a Byzantine emperor if the sagas are believed, and burned Hedeby. He died with an arrow in the throat, charging, at fifty-one.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Last Viking King, likes leaders with strong navies and dislikes those without; he crossed the North Sea with three hundred ships.

leaders.bio_codex: Harald Sigurdsson was half-brother to Olaf II of Norway and fought beside him at Stiklestad in 1030, where Olaf was killed and Harald, wounded at fifteen, escaped east. He served Yaroslav of Kiev and then, from about 1034, the Byzantine emperors as a commander of the Varangian Guard, campaigning in Sicily and the Balkans and amassing a fortune. He returned north in 1045, married Yaroslav's daughter, and forced his nephew Magnus to share the Norwegian crown; Magnus died a year later and Harald ruled alone. He fought Denmark for fifteen years without taking it, founded Oslo, and crushed the old chieftains at home, earning the name Hardrada. In 1066, invited by Tostig Godwinson, he invaded England to claim its throne. He won at Fulford and five days later, on 25 September, was killed at Stamford Bridge by Harold Godwinson's army. Three weeks after that Harold fell at Hastings. The Viking age is usually dated to end with Harald.
leaders.legacy: He fought from Kiev to Sicily to York, and his death at Stamford Bridge is where historians end the Viking age.

leaders.name: Hojo Tokimune

personality.temperament: He was eighteen when the Mongol envoys came, and he had them turned away; when they came again he had them beheaded. He studied Zen with Chinese masters, built Engaku-ji for the dead of both sides, and is said to have asked his teacher Mugaku Sogen how to face the invasion and been told to cut off the source of fear. He answered the Mongols with walls and with a refusal that did not change.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Bushido, likes leaders whose faith and culture match their military strength and dislikes those who field armies without them.

leaders.bio_codex: Hōjō Tokimune was born in 1251, the son of the regent Tokiyori, and became shikken, regent for a child shogun and the real ruler of Japan, in 1268 at eighteen. That year Kublai Khan's envoys arrived demanding submission. Tokimune refused them. In November 1274 a Mongol-Korean fleet landed in Hakata Bay with perhaps thirty thousand men, fought a day against the samurai of Kyushu, and withdrew in a storm. Tokimune executed the next embassies, in 1275 and 1279, and built a stone wall twenty kilometres long around the bay. In the summer of 1281 two fleets, some four thousand ships and a hundred and forty thousand men by the chronicles, were held on the beaches for seven weeks and then destroyed by a typhoon, the kamikaze, the divine wind. Tokimune founded Engaku-ji in Kamakura to pray for the dead of both sides, and died in 1284 at thirty-three. The shogunate, unable to pay the samurai who had fought, outlived him by fifty years.
leaders.legacy: He refused the Mongols twice and the sea finished the argument; Japan was not invaded again for seven centuries.

leaders.name: Jadwiga

personality.temperament: She was crowned king, not queen, at ten, so that no husband could claim the crown over her. At twelve she gave up the Habsburg prince she had been promised and married the pagan grand duke of Lithuania, who was baptised for the purpose, and the chronicles treat the marriage as a sacrifice she made for the conversion of a nation. She spoke six languages, founded a theology faculty at Kraków, and sold her jewels to refound the university. She died at twenty-five, days after her only child.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Saint, likes leaders who follow her religion and dislikes those who spread another; her marriage converted Lithuania, the last pagan state in Europe.

leaders.bio_codex: Jadwiga was the younger daughter of Louis I of Hungary and Poland, of the Angevin house, and was crowned at Kraków in October 1384 at the age of ten with the title of king, since Polish law knew no reigning queen. The Polish lords broke her childhood betrothal to William of Habsburg and in 1386 married her to Jogaila, grand duke of Lithuania, who accepted baptism as Władysław and was crowned beside her. The union of the two crowns created the largest state in Europe and lasted, in one form or another, until 1795. She ruled in her own right, negotiating with the Teutonic Knights, reconciling Jogaila with his cousin Vytautas, and leading an army into Ruthenia in 1387. She was a patron of scholars and translators and endowed the University of Kraków from her estate. She died on 17 July 1399, weeks after giving birth to a daughter who did not live. Poland venerated her at once; the Church canonised her in 1997.
leaders.legacy: She was crowned king at ten, married for a nation's conversion at twelve, and died at twenty-five a saint.

leaders.name: Jayavarman VII

personality.temperament: His face is the one carved two hundred times on the towers of the Bayon, eyes half closed, mouth in a slight smile, and probably his portrait. He came to power late, after the Cham had sacked Angkor, drove them out and built more in thirty-seven years than any Khmer king before him: a walled city, a temple for his mother, a temple for his father, a hundred hospitals, rest houses along every road. An inscription says he suffered from the illnesses of his subjects more than from his own.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Monsoon Season, likes leaders with large city populations and dislikes those with small ones; his reign fed Angkor's million from its reservoirs.

leaders.bio_codex: Jayavarman was a prince of the Khmer royal house who spent his middle years in Champa, the kingdom on the coast of what is now Vietnam, and was nearly sixty when a Cham fleet sailed up the Tonlé Sap and sacked Angkor in 1177. He returned, raised an army, defeated the Cham on the lake and in the field, and was crowned in 1181. He then invaded Champa itself and ruled it for twenty years. At home he built Angkor Thom, a walled capital with the Bayon at its centre, and the temple monasteries of Ta Prohm and Preah Khan, dedicated to his mother and father; he built one hundred and two hospitals and one hundred and twenty-one rest houses, and roads with stone bridges to link them. He made Mahayana Buddhism the state religion in a Hindu kingdom. The building emptied the treasury and the labour of a generation, and his successors reversed his faith and defaced his images. He died around 1218, in his nineties.
leaders.legacy: He rebuilt Angkor from a sack and left more stone, more hospitals and more roads than any king of Cambodia.
leaders.expansion_origin: Khmer and Indonesia Civilization & Scenario Pack

leaders.name: João III
leaders.polity: Kingdom of Portugal and its overseas empire
titles: King of Portugal and the Algarves
Lord of Guinea and of the Conquest, Navigation and Commerce of Ethiopia, Arabia, Persia and India

personality.temperament: The Pious King was not a sailor and never left Portugal. He inherited an empire of forts and factories from Lisbon to the Spice Islands and spent his reign deciding which to keep. He brought the Inquisition to Portugal, sent the Jesuits to Goa and Japan, settled Brazil with captaincies, and gave up Moroccan fortresses the crown could no longer pay for. He married his sister to Charles V and his children died before him, all nine.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Navigator's Legacy, likes leaders who settle coasts and dislikes those who keep away from the sea; Portugal's whole empire was a line of harbours.

leaders.bio_codex: João III succeeded his father Manuel I in December 1521, at nineteen, as king of a country of a million people that held the sea route to India. He reorganised the Estado da Índia, took Diu and Bassein, and opened trade with China at Macau and with Japan at Tanegashima in 1543. He divided Brazil into hereditary captaincies in 1534 and, when most of them failed, sent a royal governor to found Salvador in 1549. He invited the Society of Jesus to Portugal in 1540 and sent Francis Xavier east; he obtained the Inquisition from Rome in 1536 and it burned its first heretics in Lisbon in 1540. He abandoned Safim, Azamor and Arzila in Morocco, judging them unaffordable, and he fell into debt to the bankers of Antwerp for the rest. He died in June 1557, outlived by none of his children; the crown passed to his grandson Sebastião, a child of three.
leaders.legacy: He turned an age of discovery into an empire of administration, from Brazil to Japan, and buried every heir he had.

leaders.name: John Curtin
titles: Leader of the Australian Labor Party

personality.temperament: He was a socialist newspaperman who had gone to prison for opposing conscription in 1916 and who, as prime minister, introduced it. He had fought drink and lost for years, then won. He walked the grounds of the Lodge at night during the Battle of the Coral Sea, unable to sleep. He told the country, in the week after Pearl Harbor, that Australia looked to America, free of any pangs about its links with Britain, and Churchill did not forgive him.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Perpetually on Guard, likes leaders who liberate cities and dislikes those who take cities from others; he brought Australia's divisions home to defend it.

leaders.bio_codex: John Curtin was born in Creswick, Victoria, in 1885, left school at thirteen, and came up through the Victorian socialist movement and the timber workers' union. He edited the Westralian Worker in Perth, won Fremantle for Labor in 1928, and led the party from 1935. He became prime minister in October 1941 when two independents crossed the floor, and nine weeks later Japan entered the war. In December he turned to the United States over Britain's objection; in February 1942 he refused Churchill's order to divert the 7th Division to Burma and brought it home; he placed Australian forces under MacArthur's command, introduced conscription for service in the islands, and organised the economy for total war. His health broke under it. He died in office on 5 July 1945, six weeks before Japan's surrender. He is the only Australian prime minister to have died in the Lodge in wartime, and polls of historians regularly name him the country's greatest.
leaders.legacy: He turned Australia from Britain to America in a week and died before the war he directed was won.

leaders.name: Kristina
titles: Duchess of Estonia, Livonia and Karelia

personality.temperament: She was raised as a prince because her father ordered it, rode and shot and swore like one, and read ten hours a day. She brought Descartes to Stockholm and he died of the winter. She would not marry, would not stay Lutheran and would not stay queen; she abdicated at twenty-seven, rode to Rome in men's clothes, converted, and spent the rest of her life collecting paintings, manuscripts and debts. She is one of four women buried in St Peter's.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Minerva of the North, likes leaders with many Great Works and wonders and dislikes those with few; she stripped Prague's castle for her library.

leaders.bio_codex: Christina was born in Stockholm in December 1626, the only surviving child of Gustavus Adolphus, who was killed at Lützen when she was six. She was educated as a king's heir and took the government in 1644 at eighteen, during the last years of the Thirty Years' War, which the Peace of Westphalia ended in 1648 with Sweden a great power. She made her court a university, bringing Descartes, Grotius, Salmasius and Vossius to Stockholm and filling the castle with the libraries and galleries her armies had taken from Prague. In June 1654 she abdicated in favour of her cousin Charles Gustav, left Sweden within days, and in 1655 was received into the Catholic Church at Innsbruck. She settled in Rome, founded the academy that became the Arcadia, patronised Scarlatti and Corelli and Bernini, intrigued for the crowns of Naples and Poland, and had her equerry Monaldeschi executed at Fontainebleau for betraying her. She died in Rome in 1689.
leaders.legacy: She gave up a crown to keep her mind her own and made Rome's greatest private collection with Sweden's spoils.

leaders.name: Kupe

dates.historicity: legendary; the settlement of Aotearoa c. 1250 to 1300 is historical

leaders.polity: Hawaiki (the ancestral Polynesian homeland); Aotearoa (New Zealand)

personality.temperament: The traditions differ by iwi, but they agree on the ocean. He left Hawaiki in the canoe Matahourua, chasing a great octopus that had stolen his people's bait, or fleeing a quarrel over a woman, and found a long white cloud on the horizon that his wife named Aotearoa. He sailed its coasts and named its places, Castlepoint, Mana, the Hokianga where he turned for home. He went back to Hawaiki with the sailing directions. He did not return.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Kaitiakitanga, likes leaders who keep their land's appeal high and dislikes those who strip it; his descendants are the guardians of the land he found.

leaders.bio_codex: Kupe is the navigator credited in many Māori traditions with the discovery of Aotearoa. The stories place his homeland in Hawaiki, the ancestral land of Polynesian memory, and give him a double-hulled voyaging canoe, the Matahourua, a wife Kuramārōtini, and a companion or rival, Ngake. He is said to have followed the long-tailed cuckoo south, found the islands empty of people, named the coasts and the harbours, fought the octopus of Muturangi in Cook Strait, and sailed home with the star path, the Hokianga-nui-a-Kupe, the great returning place of Kupe, marking where he left. Later voyages of the great fleet followed his directions. Archaeology dates the first settlement of New Zealand to about 1250 to 1300 CE, the last large landmass on Earth to be settled by people, and the wayfinding by stars, swells and birds that the tradition describes is how it was done. Kupe's name is on the land in a dozen places and on no stone.
leaders.legacy: He found the last empty land on Earth and left the directions so that others could.

leaders.name: Lady Six Sky

personality.temperament: The stelae of Naranjo show her standing on a bound captive, in the pose and dress of a king, and name her Ix Wak Chan Ajaw, Lady Six Sky. She came from Dos Pilas at nineteen to restart a dynasty that war had ended, never took the royal title, and ruled through a son she had at five years old crowned. For forty years the inscriptions record her wars. No other Maya woman left so many monuments.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Solitary, likes leaders who settle away from her and dislikes those who settle near her capital; Naranjo's wars were all with its neighbours.

leaders.bio_codex: Wak Chanil Ajaw was a daughter of the king of Dos Pilas, a branch of the Tikal royal line allied to Calakmul, and in August 682 CE she arrived at Naranjo, a city in the Petén whose ruling house had been destroyed in war with Caracol. She took the government without the title of ajaw, performed the rituals of a king, and in 693 installed her five-year-old son K'ahk' Tiliw Chan Chaak on the throne. The monuments of the next decades record campaigns against Ucanal, Yaxha, Tuubal and others, a string of victories that rebuilt Naranjo's standing in the lowlands. Her stelae show her trampling captives, a pose otherwise reserved for male rulers, and record her bloodletting rites at the turning of the calendar. She outlived her son, who died in 728, and governed on into old age. Her last recorded date is 741. The Maya collapse took Naranjo within a century and a half of her death.
leaders.legacy: She rebuilt a destroyed kingdom from the throne she never claimed and left more monuments than any Maya queen.
leaders.expansion_origin: New Frontier Pass: Maya & Gran Colombia Pack

leaders.name: Lautaro

personality.temperament: He was taken as a boy to be a Spanish officer's groom and spent three years watching horses, muskets and the way the invaders fought. Then he went home and taught his people to fight back in relays, to lure cavalry into ground that horses could not cross, and to ride the horses they captured. He killed the governor who had owned him. He was twenty-three when a surprise attack at dawn ended him, and the war he started lasted three hundred years.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Spirit of Tucapel, likes leaders who keep their cities loyal and dislikes those who lose them; he fought the Spanish for the land itself.

leaders.bio_codex: Lautaro, Leftraru in Mapudungun, was captured around 1546 at the age of about eleven and served Pedro de Valdivia, conqueror and governor of Chile, as a page and groom. He escaped in 1550 or 1551 with a knowledge of Spanish horsemanship, armour and tactics. The Mapuche elected him toqui in 1553. At Tucapel in December of that year he attacked Valdivia's column in waves, exhausting the Spanish horse, destroyed it, and killed Valdivia. At Marihueñu in 1554 he destroyed a second army and burned Concepción, and burned it again in 1555. In 1556 he marched north on Santiago itself, through plague and famine, and in April 1557, camped on the Mataquito river, was surprised at dawn by Francisco de Villagra's cavalry and killed with most of his men. His head was displayed in Santiago. The Arauco War he began did not end until the 1880s, and Chile named warships, streets and a lodge of independence after him.
leaders.legacy: He learned the invaders' war as their servant and turned it on them, and the Mapuche held their land for three centuries after.

leaders.name: Ludwig II
leaders.polity: Kingdom of Bavaria (within the German Empire from 1871)

personality.temperament: He came to the throne at eighteen, tall and handsome, and within weeks had summoned Wagner, whose debts he paid and whose operas he staged for himself alone. He withdrew from Munich and from people, slept by day, drove through the mountains at night in a gilded sleigh, and built castles he never finished and could not afford: Neuschwanstein on its crag, Linderhof with its grotto, Herrenchiemsee copied from Versailles. His ministers had him declared insane. He drowned in a lake the next day with the doctor who had certified him.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Dreamer of the Mountain, likes leaders who build wonders and dislikes those who let their cities fall into disrepair; he built three castles and bankrupted himself.

leaders.bio_codex: Ludwig became king of Bavaria in March 1864 on his father's sudden death. He was eighteen, unprepared, and devoted to Richard Wagner, whom he brought to Munich and financed through Tristan, Die Meistersinger and the building of Bayreuth. Bavaria fought on Austria's side in 1866 and lost; in 1870 Ludwig's letter proposing the Prussian king as German emperor, written at Bismarck's dictation in exchange for a secret pension, made Bavaria a state within the German Empire. He withdrew from government and from the capital. From 1869 he built Neuschwanstein, from 1874 Linderhof, from 1878 Herrenchiemsee, borrowing against the civil list until his debts reached fourteen million marks and his ministers, fearing he would sell Bavaria to pay them, had him deposed as insane on 10 June 1886. On 13 June he was found dead in the shallows of Lake Starnberg with Dr Gudden, his examiner. The castles he built on credit are now Bavaria's largest source of tourist income.
leaders.legacy: He ruined a treasury on castles for an audience of one, and the castles now pay for Bavaria.

leaders.name: Mansa Musa
titles: Lord of the Mines of Wangara

personality.temperament: He went to Mecca in 1324 with sixty thousand people and a hundred camels of gold, gave so much away in Cairo that the price of gold fell for a decade, and came back with architects and scholars. Arab writers who met him describe a man of dignity and few words who kept a hall of silent audience and would not be seen to eat. His empire ran on salt from the north and gold from the south and the law of the Quran at every stop between.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Gold and Salt, likes leaders who send him trade routes and dislikes those who do not; the whole of Mali was built on the caravans.

leaders.bio_codex: Musa came to the throne of Mali in 1312 when his predecessor Abu Bakr II sailed into the Atlantic with a fleet and did not come back, or so Musa told the Egyptians. Mali already held the gold fields of Bambuk and Bure and the salt mines of Taghaza; Musa extended it to Gao and Timbuktu and governed it through provincial governors and a standing army. In 1324 he made the pilgrimage to Mecca by way of Cairo, where his spending in gold dust and gifts flooded the market and depressed the metal's value for years; the chronicler al-Umari recorded it a dozen years later from witnesses. He returned with the Andalusian architect al-Sahili and with Maliki jurists, built the Djinguereber mosque at Timbuktu and the great mosque at Gao, and made Timbuktu a centre of learning. The Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows him seated on a throne in the middle of Africa holding a nugget. He died around 1337. His wealth is beyond estimate, which is why it is called the greatest in history.
leaders.legacy: He took so much gold to Mecca that Cairo's markets did not recover for years, and he came back with scholars.

leaders.name: Matthias Corvinus
leaders.polity: Kingdom of Hungary (and Croatia, Bohemia in part, Austria)

personality.temperament: He was elected king at fourteen by nobles on the frozen Danube, having spent the previous year as a prisoner in Prague, and he spent the next thirty-two years making sure no noble could do to him what they had done to his brother. He built the first standing army in Europe since Rome, the Black Army, and paid for it by taxing everyone. He collected the second largest library in Christendom, married an Italian, and took Vienna. Hungarian folklore made him the just king who walked among the poor in disguise.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Raven King, likes leaders who levy city-state troops and dislikes those who hold the city-states he wants; the Black Army was mostly mercenary.

leaders.bio_codex: Mátyás Hunyadi was the younger son of János Hunyadi, the general who had held the Turks at Belgrade, and was elected king of Hungary in January 1458 after his elder brother had been executed by the previous king. He was fifteen. He broke the magnates who had elected him, reformed the courts and the tax system, and from about 1462 built the Black Army, a permanent force of some twenty to thirty thousand paid soldiers, largely Bohemian and German mercenaries, with artillery and a Danube flotilla. He fought the Ottomans at Jajce and Šabac but chose not to pursue a war of reconquest; he fought instead to the west, took Moravia and Silesia from Bohemia, and in 1485 captured Vienna and most of Lower Austria from the Emperor Frederick III. His court at Buda and Visegrád was the first Renaissance court north of the Alps, and his Bibliotheca Corviniana held some two thousand codices. He died in Vienna in April 1490, leaving a bastard son the nobles refused; the army was disbanded, and Hungary lost Mohács within forty years.
leaders.legacy: He raised Europe's first standing army since Rome and the greatest library north of Italy, and both were gone within a generation of his death.

leaders.name: Menelik II

dates.display: r. 1889 to 1913 as Emperor (King of Shewa from 1866)

titles: Conquering Lion of the Tribe of Judah

personality.temperament: He spent ten years as a hostage of the emperor who had killed his father, escaped, and waited twenty more to take the crown. He bought rifles from every European power that would sell them and let each one think he was its client. When Italy claimed a treaty made Ethiopia its protectorate he denounced the Italian text, marched north with a hundred thousand men, and at Adwa destroyed the only European army ever beaten decisively by an African one in the age of empire. He then built a railway, a bank, a school and a telephone.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Mountain Lion, likes leaders who settle on hills and dislikes those who settle in his highlands; Ethiopia's independence was its mountains.

leaders.bio_codex: Sahle Maryam was born in 1844, heir to the kingdom of Shewa, and was held at the court of Emperor Tewodros II from 1855 to 1865, when he escaped and took his father's throne. He expanded Shewa south and east, founded Addis Ababa in 1886, and was crowned emperor of Ethiopia in 1889 as Menelik II on the death of Yohannes IV. That year he signed the Treaty of Wuchale with Italy; the Italian text made Ethiopia a protectorate, the Amharic did not, and when Rome insisted he repudiated it in 1893. At Adwa on 1 March 1896 his army of about a hundred thousand destroyed an Italian force of seventeen thousand, and Italy recognised Ethiopia's full independence by the treaty of October. He then doubled the empire's territory by conquest in the south, conquests that his subjects there remember as such, and brought in the Djibouti railway, the first bank, the first modern school, electricity and the telephone. A stroke left him incapable from 1909; he died in December 1913.
leaders.legacy: He beat a European army at Adwa and kept Ethiopia the one African state that was never a colony.

leaders.name: Montezuma

dates.historicity: historical; Civ VI's Montezuma draws on both Moctezuma I and II

titles: Ilhuicamina (He Who Shoots Arrows at the Sky)

personality.temperament: The game's Montezuma, with his feathers and his hunger for luxuries, is a composite, but the conqueror who built the empire was the first of the name. Moctezuma Ilhuicamina took the Triple Alliance beyond the Valley of Mexico, codified its laws, decreed the sumptuary rules that told each rank what it could wear, and after famine instituted the flower wars that fed the temples with captives. He raised the Great Temple and built the aqueduct from Chapultepec. The captives are part of the record, not a footnote.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Tribute, wants the luxuries his neighbours have and resents those who hold them; the Aztec state ran on tribute lists.

leaders.bio_codex: Moctezuma Ilhuicamina was born around 1398, the son of the tlatoani Huitzilihuitl, and was elected ruler of Tenochtitlan in 1440 after serving his half-brother Itzcoatl as general and chief adviser. With Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco he pushed the Triple Alliance south across the mountains into Morelos and east to the Gulf coast, bringing Chalco, Cuauhnahuac and the Huastec cities under tribute. The great famine of 1450 to 1454 nearly broke the city; afterwards he and his adviser Tlacaelel formalised the xochiyaoyotl, the flower wars with Tlaxcala and Huexotzinco fought to take prisoners for sacrifice. He rebuilt the Templo Mayor, built the dike of Nezahualcoyotl across the lake against floods, laid the aqueduct from Chapultepec, founded the botanical garden at Huaxtepec and issued the sumptuary laws that ordered Aztec society by dress. He died in 1469. His great-grandson Moctezuma II, who received Cortés, carried the name to its end.
leaders.legacy: He made Tenochtitlan an empire and gave it the laws, the temple and the wars that defined it until the Spanish came.

leaders.name: Nzinga Mbande
leaders.faith: Mbundu religion; baptised Catholic 1622, returned to the Church 1656

personality.temperament: At her first negotiation with the Portuguese governor in Luanda she was offered no chair, so a servant knelt and she sat on his back for the meeting. She was baptised when it helped, allied with the Dutch when it helped, led her soldiers in person into her sixties, and kept the Portuguese out of Matamba for thirty years. Her brother's murder, which she may have arranged, and the Imbangala alliance, with its sacrifices, are in the record beside the resistance.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Decolonization, likes leaders who keep their cities on their home continent and dislikes those who settle on hers; she fought Portugal's colony for forty years.

leaders.bio_codex: Nzinga was born about 1583, a daughter of the ngola of Ndongo, a Mbundu kingdom inland from the Portuguese colony at Luanda. In 1622 she represented her brother at Luanda and negotiated a treaty that recognised Ndongo's independence; she was baptised Ana de Sousa there. When her brother died in 1624, by her hand according to some accounts, she took the throne. The Portuguese broke the treaty and drove her out in 1626; she allied with the Imbangala war bands, took the kingdom of Matamba in 1631, and from there fought Portugal for thirty years, allying with the Dutch during their occupation of Luanda from 1641 to 1648 and defeating a Portuguese army at Ngoleme in 1644. She made peace in 1656, returned to the Church with Capuchin missionaries at her court, and governed Matamba until her death in December 1663 at about eighty. Angola's independence movement took her as a founding figure three centuries later.
leaders.legacy: She held the Portuguese at the edge of Angola for forty years with every alliance the age offered, and died a queen at eighty.

leaders.name: Pachacuti

dates.historicity: historical; from Spanish-era chronicles of Inca oral history

personality.temperament: His name means he who overturns the world, and the chroniclers say he took it after the day the Chanka came for Cusco and his father and elder brother fled. He stayed, won, and remade everything: the city in the shape of a puma, the sun temple sheathed in gold, the roads, the storehouses, the census, the calendar, Machu Picchu as his estate. He moved whole peoples across the mountains to break resistance. He retired and let his son conquer.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Sapa Inca, likes leaders who stay off his continent and dislikes those who settle on it; Tawantinsuyu meant the four quarters of the world.

leaders.bio_codex: Cusi Yupanqui was a younger son of the Inca Viracocha, ruler of the small Cusco kingdom in the Andes. When the Chanka confederation attacked Cusco around 1438 and his father withdrew, he led the defence, won, and took the throne and the name Pachacuti. In thirty years he turned Cusco into Tawantinsuyu, conquering the Titicaca basin, the central highlands and the coast, and sending his son Topa Inca north to Quito. He rebuilt Cusco in stone, raised the Coricancha to the sun, and ordered the terraces, storehouses, roads and way stations that let the state move armies and grain across four thousand kilometres of mountain. He resettled conquered peoples as mitimaes far from home, fixed the quipu records and the labour tax, and built the royal estate at Machu Picchu. He gave up the campaigns to his son around 1463 and died in Cusco in 1471. Sixty years later Pizarro's men found the empire he had made and took it in two years.
leaders.legacy: He turned a mountain town into the largest empire in the Americas and built the roads that are still there.

leaders.name: Pedro II

personality.temperament: He became emperor at five when his father sailed for Portugal, and he was crowned at fourteen because the regents could not keep order. He spoke a dozen languages, corresponded with Darwin, Pasteur and Victor Hugo, sat in the front row at Wagner's Bayreuth, and visited Alexander Graham Bell's stall at Philadelphia and said, my God, it talks. He freed the slaves by proxy and was deposed by the army a year later. He died in a Paris hotel with a pillow of Brazilian earth.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Magnanimous, likes leaders who recruit Great People and does not begrudge them; he spent his reign among scientists and poets.

leaders.bio_codex: Pedro de Alcântara was born in Rio de Janeiro in December 1825 and became emperor of Brazil in April 1831 at the age of five when his father, Pedro I, abdicated. A troubled regency ended with his early majority in 1840. For the next forty-nine years he governed a constitutional monarchy larger than Europe, with a parliament, a free press and a court that imported science and opera; he founded institutes, schools and observatories and travelled abroad three times, the first Brazilian ruler to do so. He fought Paraguay in the War of the Triple Alliance from 1864 to 1870 at great cost. He pushed the abolition of slavery by degrees, the free womb law of 1871 and the Golden Law of 1888 signed by his daughter Isabel while he was in Europe. The planters who had lost their slaves and the officers who wanted a republic deposed him on 15 November 1889; he went into exile without resistance and died in Paris in December 1891. Brazil brought his body home in 1921.
leaders.legacy: He ruled Brazil for half a century as a scholar-emperor, ended slavery, and was sent into exile for it.

leaders.name: Pericles

dates.display: leading statesman of Athens c. 461 to 429 BCE

leaders.polity: Athenian democracy and the Delian League

personality.temperament: Thucydides, who heard him, said Athens under him was in name a democracy and in fact the rule of its first citizen. He was elected general fifteen years running and never took a bribe. He kept one friend's circle, Anaxagoras, Phidias, Aspasia, and spoke in public rarely, so that each speech landed. The comic poets called him the onion-head for the shape of his skull and the Olympian for his thunder. He buried two sons in the plague before it took him.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Delian League, likes leaders who leave the city-states he holds alone and dislikes those who compete for them; the League was Athens' empire.

leaders.bio_codex: Pericles was born around 495 BCE to Xanthippus, the victor of Mycale, and Agariste of the Alcmaeonid house. He entered politics in the 460s, prosecuted Cimon, backed the reforms of Ephialtes that stripped the Areopagus, and after Ephialtes was murdered in 461 led the democratic party for thirty years. He had the citizens paid for jury service, limited citizenship to those born of two Athenians, moved the treasury of the Delian League from Delos to Athens in 454 and spent it on the Parthenon, the Propylaea and the Odeon. He made peace with Persia and a thirty-year truce with Sparta, planted colonies, and put down Samos. When the truce broke in 431 he brought the whole population inside the Long Walls and let Attica burn, trusting the fleet. The plague of 430 killed a quarter of the city, including his sons; the assembly fined him, re-elected him, and in 429 the plague killed him. The war he started lasted twenty-seven years and Athens lost it.
leaders.legacy: He led Athens for thirty years, built the Parthenon with the League's money, and began the war that ended Athenian power.

quote.text: Our constitution is called a democracy because power is in the hands not of a minority but of the whole people.
quote.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 2.37, the Funeral Oration

leaders.name: Peter

dates.display: r. 1682 to 1725 (sole rule from 1696; Emperor from 1721)

leaders.polity: Tsardom of Russia; Russian Empire from 1721

personality.temperament: He stood over two metres tall, worked as a ship's carpenter in Holland under a false name, pulled teeth as a hobby, drank with a mock synod of drunkards, and shaved the beards off his nobles with his own hand. He built a capital on a swamp and ordered his subjects into it. He had his son tortured to death for treason. He learned everything he could from the West and used it against everyone who stood in his way, which included most of Russia.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Westernizer, likes leaders who lead him in science and culture and dislikes those behind him; he went to Europe to learn and came back to force it.

leaders.bio_codex: Peter Alexeyevich was born in 1672 and proclaimed tsar at ten, jointly with his half-brother Ivan and under the regency of his half-sister Sophia, whom he overthrew in 1689. He took Azov from the Turks in 1696 and in 1697 travelled through Europe incognito, working in the Dutch and English shipyards and recruiting engineers. He came home to crush the streltsy revolt with mass executions and to force Western dress, the Julian calendar and a beard tax on the boyars. In 1700 he went to war with Sweden; after the defeat at Narva he rebuilt the army on European lines, founded St Petersburg on the Neva marsh in 1703, and at Poltava in 1709 destroyed Charles XII's army. The peace of Nystad in 1721 gave Russia the Baltic coast and Peter the title of emperor. He built the navy, the Senate, the Table of Ranks, the Academy of Sciences and the first Russian newspaper. His son Alexei died under interrogation in 1718. Peter died in February 1725, at fifty-two, without naming an heir.
leaders.legacy: He dragged Russia into Europe by the beard and built its capital on a marsh with the bones of the men who dug it.

leaders.name: Philip II
leaders.polity: Spanish Empire (Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Naples, Sicily, Milan, the Americas, the Philippines)

personality.temperament: He governed the first empire on which the sun never set from a desk, reading and annotating every dispatch himself, in a monastery-palace he built in the hills above Madrid with his bedroom opening onto the high altar. He married four times, lost Elizabeth of England to heresy and the Netherlands to revolt, bankrupted the treasury four times, and sent an Armada that the wind destroyed. He wore black and distrusted everyone, including, with reason, his secretaries.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Counter Reformer, likes leaders who follow his religion and will not tolerate those who spread another into his cities; the Spanish Inquisition was his instrument.

leaders.bio_codex: Philip was born at Valladolid in 1527, the son of the Emperor Charles V, and was raised to rule from childhood. His father gave him Naples and Milan, then the Netherlands, then in 1556 Spain and the Indies. He had married Mary I of England in 1554 and was king consort there until her death in 1558. He won at Saint-Quentin, built El Escorial from 1563 as palace, monastery and tomb, and from 1568 fought the revolt of the Netherlands that his taxation and his heresy laws had provoked; the Duke of Alba's Council of Blood executed over a thousand. His fleet beat the Turks at Lepanto in 1571. In 1580 he took the Portuguese crown by inheritance and arms. In 1588 he sent the Armada against Elizabeth and lost a third of it. He defaulted on his debts in 1557, 1560, 1575 and 1596, the silver of Potosí notwithstanding. He died at El Escorial in September 1598 after fifty-three days of illness, having governed for forty-two years with a pen.
leaders.legacy: He ruled the first global empire from a desk in a monastery and bankrupted it four times in the service of his faith.

leaders.name: Qin Shi Huang

dates.display: King of Qin 247 to 221 BCE; First Emperor 221 to 210 BCE

leaders.polity: State of Qin; the Qin dynasty, first unified Chinese empire
leaders.faith: Chinese state religion; Legalism in governance; sought immortality through alchemy

personality.temperament: He took the title huangdi, august sovereign, because king was no longer large enough. He standardised the script, the axle width, the weights and the coinage, burned the books that disagreed with him and, the histories say, buried the scholars who wrote them. He survived three assassination attempts and stopped sleeping in the same palace twice. He sent expeditions for the elixir of life and drank mercury for it. He was buried under a mountain with an army of clay.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Wall of 10,000 Li, dislikes leaders who build more wonders than he does; his tomb complex employed seven hundred thousand labourers.

leaders.bio_codex: Ying Zheng was born in 259 BCE at Handan, a hostage prince's son, and became king of Qin at thirteen in 247. He took the government at twenty-two, dismissed his regent Lü Buwei, and with the Legalist minister Li Si and the generals Wang Jian and Meng Tian destroyed the six rival kingdoms one by one between 230 and 221 BCE. He proclaimed himself Shi Huangdi, First Emperor, abolished the feudal states for thirty-six commanderies, unified the writing system, the currency, the measures and the width of cart axles, built roads and canals, and joined the northern walls into a single frontier against the Xiongnu. In 213 he had the histories and classics of the other states burned; in 212, by Sima Qian's account, he had four hundred and sixty scholars buried alive. He toured his empire five times seeking immortality from magicians and died on the fifth tour, in 210 BCE, probably of the mercury he took. His dynasty fell four years later. His tomb at Lintong, guarded by eight thousand terracotta soldiers, has not been opened.
leaders.legacy: He made one China out of seven kingdoms and one script out of many, and his dynasty outlived him by four years.

leaders.name: Robert the Bruce

personality.temperament: He changed sides three times in the wars with Edward I before he killed his rival John Comyn at the altar of Greyfriars in Dumfries and had himself crowned six weeks later. He lost two battles in a year, lost three brothers to the executioner, and spent a winter in hiding, where the spider is said to have taught him to try again. He won by burning castles rather than holding them and by choosing the one battle he could win. He died of leprosy, or something like it, and asked that his heart be carried to the Holy Land.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Flower of Scotland, dislikes leaders who declare war on his neighbours and will fight for them; he spent his reign fighting for one.

leaders.bio_codex: Robert Bruce was born in 1274, heir to the earldom of Carrick and the Bruce claim to the Scottish throne that Edward I of England had rejected in favour of John Balliol. He served Edward, then Wallace, then Edward again. On 10 February 1306 he met John Comyn, his rival claimant, in the church of the Greyfriars at Dumfries and killed him, and on 25 March was crowned at Scone. He was beaten at Methven and Dalry that summer and fled to the western isles while Edward hanged his supporters and imprisoned his wife and daughter. From 1307 he fought a guerrilla war, recovered the north, and razed every castle he took. Edward I died marching against him. On 23 and 24 June 1314 at Bannockburn he destroyed Edward II's army, twice his size, in the marshes below Stirling. The Declaration of Arbroath in 1320 told the pope that Scotland would never be subject to England; the treaty of Edinburgh in 1328 made England agree. He died at Cardross in June 1329.
leaders.legacy: He took a crown by murder, lost everything, and won it back at Bannockburn so completely that England signed.

leaders.name: Saladin

dates.display: Sultan of Egypt from 1171; Sultan of Egypt and Syria 1174 to 1193

leaders.polity: Ayyubid Sultanate (Egypt, Syria, Upper Mesopotamia, Hejaz, Yemen)

personality.temperament: A Kurdish soldier's son who did not want Egypt and was sent there by his uncle, he found himself vizier of a Shia caliphate and quietly ended it. He gave away so much that his treasury held one gold piece when he died. He took Jerusalem without a massacre, ransomed the poor, and let the Christians leave with their goods; the crusaders had killed everyone in it eighty-eight years before. He sent Richard the Lionheart fruit and snow when he was ill and two horses when his was killed. He had the Templars and Hospitallers beheaded after Hattin.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Ayyubid Dynasty, likes leaders who follow his religion and dislikes those who hold cities of another faith near him; he spent his life gathering Islam's lands against the crusaders.

leaders.bio_codex: Yusuf ibn Ayyub was born at Tikrit in 1137 or 1138 and rose in the service of Nur ad-Din of Damascus. Sent to Egypt with his uncle Shirkuh in 1164, he succeeded him as vizier to the Fatimid caliph in 1169 and in 1171 abolished the Fatimid caliphate, restoring Egypt to Sunni allegiance. On Nur ad-Din's death in 1174 he took Damascus, then Aleppo in 1183 and Mosul in 1186, uniting the Muslim lands around the crusader kingdom for the first time. On 4 July 1187 at the Horns of Hattin he destroyed the army of Jerusalem, and on 2 October the city surrendered on terms. The Third Crusade followed; Richard of England retook Acre and beat him at Arsuf, but could not take Jerusalem, and the treaty of 1192 left it in Saladin's hands with the coast to the Franks. He died in Damascus on 4 March 1193 and was buried beside the Umayyad mosque. Dante put him in Limbo among the virtuous pagans, the only Muslim ruler Europe chose to admire.
leaders.legacy: He united Egypt and Syria, retook Jerusalem without a massacre, and died with one gold coin in the treasury.

leaders.name: Seondeok

personality.temperament: The Samguk Sagi gives her three prophecies: that a painted peony had no scent because the Chinese had sent no butterflies, that frogs croaking at a jade gate meant soldiers hiding in a valley, and the day of her own death. She built the oldest observatory still standing in East Asia and a nine-storey wooden pagoda meant to subdue nine enemies. A rebellion rose against her in her last year for being a woman; she died while it was being put down.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Cheomseongdae, likes leaders who invest in science and dislikes those who lag; she built an observatory before she built walls.

leaders.bio_codex: Deokman was the eldest daughter of King Jinpyeong of Silla, who died in 632 without a son, and she succeeded him under the rule that only those of the sacred bone rank could reign. Silla was the smallest of the three Korean kingdoms and at war with both Baekje and Goguryeo; she sent students and envoys to Tang China, secured its alliance, and raised the general Kim Yu-sin and the statesman Kim Chunchu who would, under her successors, unify the peninsula. She built the Cheomseongdae observatory at Gyeongju, a bottle-shaped tower of 362 stones that still stands, the Hwangnyongsa nine-storey pagoda, the tallest wooden structure in Asia until the Mongols burned it, and the temple of Bunhwangsa. In 647 the noble Bidam rebelled, declaring that a woman could not rule; Kim Yu-sin crushed the rising, and Seondeok died in the same month, on the day she had foretold. Her cousin Jindeok, a second queen, followed her.
leaders.legacy: She ruled a kingdom at war with both its neighbours, built the oldest observatory in Asia, and set up the men who unified Korea.

leaders.name: Shaka

personality.temperament: He was an illegitimate son driven out with his mother, and he came back with a short stabbing spear and a new way of fighting. He drilled his regiments barefoot over thorns, forbade them to marry, and ordered the enemy's wounded killed and his own cowards executed on the field. He built a kingdom of a quarter of a million in a decade. When his mother died he ordered the nation to mourn for a year without crops or milk, and had thousands killed for not weeping enough. His half-brothers stabbed him.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Paramount Chief, likes leaders who form corps and armies and dislikes those with scattered units; the impi fought as a single body.

leaders.bio_codex: Shaka was born around 1787 to Senzangakhona, chief of the small Zulu clan, and Nandi, a Langeni woman, in a union his father's people did not recognise. Mother and son were driven out and he grew up among the Mthethwa, where he became a soldier of Dingiswayo. He took the Zulu chieftaincy about 1816 with Dingiswayo's backing and replaced the throwing spear with the iklwa, a short stabbing blade, replaced sandals with bare feet for speed, and organised his men into age regiments with the bull-horn formation of a centre and two enveloping wings. By 1824 he ruled from the Pongola to the Tugela and his wars had set the whole interior in motion, the mfecane, which emptied and remade southern Africa. He received the first British traders at Port Natal and sent envoys to the Cape. His mother Nandi died in 1827 and his grief became terror. On 22 September 1828 his half-brothers Dingane and Mhlangana murdered him at his kraal. Dingane took the kingdom.
leaders.legacy: He made a clan of a few thousand into a nation and an army, and the shock of it reorganised half a continent.

leaders.name: Simón Bolívar
leaders.polity: Gran Colombia (Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama); Peru; Bolivia

personality.temperament: He was a rich orphan who swore on a hill in Rome to free his country and spent the fortune doing it. He crossed the Andes in winter with an army in rags, lost and won and lost again, and freed six countries. He wrote the constitution of Bolivia with a president for life and watched the republics he made turn on each other and on him. He said that he who serves a revolution ploughs the sea. He died of tuberculosis on the way to exile, forty-seven, with his boots and shirt borrowed.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Campaña Admirable, likes leaders who keep their units close to home and dislikes those who send armies near his borders; his wars were liberations and he read any other army as an invasion.

leaders.bio_codex: Simón Bolívar was born in Caracas in 1783 to one of the richest families in Venezuela, orphaned by nine, and educated by the republican tutor Simón Rodríguez and in Europe. He joined the junta that deposed the Spanish governor in 1810 and, after the first republic fell, led the Admirable Campaign of 1813 that retook Caracas. He was driven out again in 1814, wrote the Jamaica Letter from exile, returned with Haitian help in 1816, and in 1819 crossed the flooded llanos and the Andes to beat the Spanish at Boyacá and take Bogotá. He proclaimed Gran Colombia and won Venezuela at Carabobo in 1821; Sucre won Ecuador at Pichincha in 1822; Bolívar won Peru at Junín in 1824 and Sucre finished it at Ayacucho. Upper Peru became Bolivia in his name in 1825. The union then came apart: Venezuela seceded, an assassination attempt in 1828 nearly killed him, and in 1830 he resigned and set out for Europe. He died at Santa Marta on 17 December 1830.
leaders.legacy: He freed six nations from Spain and lived to see them refuse the union he had built for them.

quote.text: He who serves a revolution ploughs the sea.
quote.source: Letter to General Juan José Flores, 9 November 1830

leaders.expansion_origin: New Frontier Pass: Maya & Gran Colombia Pack

leaders.name: Suleiman

personality.temperament: Europe called him the Magnificent and his own people called him the Lawgiver, and he was both: he besieged Vienna and he wrote the code that ran the empire for three centuries. He wrote poetry under the name Muhibbi, the lover, much of it to Hürrem, the slave he freed and married against every custom. He had his friend Ibrahim strangled, his son Mustafa strangled in front of him, and died in his tent at the siege of Szigetvár, which was kept from the army until the fortress fell.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Lawgiver, likes leaders with large standing militaries and dislikes those who do not match him; the Janissaries were the first modern standing army in Europe.

leaders.bio_codex: Suleiman succeeded his father Selim I in September 1520, at twenty-five, as sultan of an empire that already held Syria and Egypt. He took Belgrade in 1521 and Rhodes from the Knights in 1522, destroyed the Hungarian army at Mohács in 1526 and killed its king, and in 1529 besieged Vienna and failed in the autumn rain. He took Baghdad from the Safavids in 1534 and most of Hungary in 1541, and his admiral Barbarossa made the Mediterranean an Ottoman sea. He rewrote the kanun, the secular law of the empire, settled the taxes and the land system, built the Süleymaniye with Sinan and rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem. He married Hürrem, a Ruthenian slave, and had his eldest son Mustafa executed in 1553 on suspicion of treason. He died on 6 September 1566, in the night, in his tent before Szigetvár, at seventy-one. The empire never again had a reign like his.
leaders.legacy: He ruled the Ottoman Empire for forty-six years at its height, besieged Vienna, and wrote the laws that outlived his line.

leaders.name: Tamar
titles: King of Kings and Queen of Queens of Georgia

personality.temperament: The chronicle of her reign calls her mepe, king, and says the nobles who made her accept a council made her accept a husband too, a Russian prince who drank and rebelled and was sent away twice. Her second husband, an Alan prince raised at her court, won her wars. She is painted in the monasteries with a long face and a long crown, and the poet Rustaveli dedicated The Knight in the Panther's Skin to her. The Church made her a saint.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Glory of the World, likes leaders who send envoys to the city-states she protects and dislikes those who take them; Georgia's golden age was an age of protectorates.

leaders.bio_codex: Tamar was crowned co-ruler by her father George III in 1178, against the opposition of the nobles, and succeeded him in 1184. The aristocracy forced her to dismiss her father's ministers, accept a council, and marry Yuri Bogolyubsky of Vladimir, whom she divorced for drunkenness in 1187 and whose two rebellions she defeated. She married David Soslan, an Alan prince, in 1189, and with him and the brothers Zakare and Ivane Mkhargrdzeli as generals won at Shamkor in 1195 and Basiani in 1203 over the Muslim rulers of Azerbaijan and Anatolia, took Kars, and in 1204 set her kinsman Alexios Komnenos on the throne of Trebizond as a client of Georgia. Her realm ran from the Black Sea to the Caspian and from the Caucasus to Erzurum. Churches, monasteries, the cave city of Vardzia and the epic of Rustaveli belong to her reign. She died in January 1213; her burial place was hidden and has not been found.
leaders.legacy: She ruled Georgia at the height of its power as king in title and queen in fact, and the Church made her a saint.

leaders.name: Teddy Roosevelt

dates.display: President of the United States 1901 to 1909

personality.temperament: He was an asthmatic child who built his body by will, a rancher, a police commissioner, a historian, a colonel who charged up a hill in Cuba, and a president at forty-two because an anarchist shot the one before him. He broke trusts, dug a canal, sent a fleet around the world, won a Nobel Prize for ending a war, and set aside 230 million acres of the public land. He was shot in the chest in 1912 and gave the speech anyway. He wanted to be in every fight, and he usually was.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Big Stick, likes leaders who keep the peace on his continent and dislikes those who start wars on it; the Roosevelt Corollary claimed the hemisphere.

leaders.bio_codex: Theodore Roosevelt was born in New York in 1858, entered the state assembly at twenty-three, lost his wife and mother on the same day in 1884, and went to the Dakota Badlands to ranch. He came back to reform the civil service and the New York police, resigned from the Navy Department in 1898 to raise the Rough Riders, and rode up San Juan Heights into the governorship of New York and the vice-presidency. McKinley's assassination made him president in September 1901. He broke up Northern Securities, mediated the coal strike, took Panama and began the canal, brokered the peace between Russia and Japan at Portsmouth, and used the Antiquities Act and the Forest Service to protect more land than any president before or since, including five national parks. He left office in 1909, hunted in Africa, split the Republicans in 1912 as a Progressive, took a bullet in the chest in Milwaukee and finished his speech, explored an unmapped river in Brazil, and died in his sleep in January 1919.
leaders.legacy: He made the presidency a bully pulpit and the national parks a national habit, and he never once stood still.

quote.text: Speak softly and carry a big stick; you will go far.
quote.source: Speech at the Minnesota State Fair, 2 September 1901, quoting what he called a West African proverb

leaders.name: Tokugawa
leaders.faith: Jōdo Buddhism; deified as a Shinto kami after death

personality.temperament: He spent his childhood as a hostage, his youth as a vassal of Nobunaga and his middle age as a vassal of Hideyoshi, and he waited. The Japanese proverb has Nobunaga pound the rice, Hideyoshi knead the dough, and Ieyasu eat the cake. He won the one battle that mattered, took the title of shogun, retired in two years so that his son's succession would be unquestioned, and then destroyed the last Toyotomi heir at Osaka. He wrote that life is like walking a long road with a heavy load, and that patience is the root of all quiet.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Sakoku, likes leaders who keep their trade and settlers away from his lands and dislikes those who send them near; his heirs closed Japan for two centuries.

leaders.bio_codex: Matsudaira Takechiyo was born at Okazaki in 1543 and spent twelve years as a hostage of the Imagawa and Oda clans. He allied with Oda Nobunaga in 1561, took the name Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1567, survived his one great defeat at Mikatagahara in 1573, and after Nobunaga's death in 1582 submitted to Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who moved him to the Kanto plain in 1590, where he built Edo. On Hideyoshi's death in 1598 he was the most powerful of the regents for the child heir, and on 21 October 1600 at Sekigahara he destroyed the western coalition in a single day. The emperor named him shogun in 1603. He abdicated in 1605 for his son Hidetada and governed from Sunpu, regulated the daimyo and the court, took control of foreign trade, began the suppression of Christianity, and in 1614 and 1615 besieged and burned Osaka Castle, ending the Toyotomi. He died in June 1616 and was enshrined at Nikkō as a god. His house ruled Japan until 1868.
leaders.legacy: He waited forty years for one battle, won it in a day, and founded a peace that lasted two hundred and fifty years.

leaders.name: Tomyris
leaders.polity: Massagetae, a Scythian people east of the Caspian

personality.temperament: Herodotus says Cyrus asked for her hand and she understood he was asking for her kingdom. She offered him a fair fight on either side of the river. He took her son by a trick, a feast with wine left for the Massagetae to find; the son killed himself in captivity. She sent Cyrus a message that she would give him his fill of blood, beat his army, and put his head in a skin of it. Herodotus had heard several versions and chose that one as the most credible.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Backstab Averse, likes leaders who keep their word and hates those who betray friends; Cyrus broke a parley to take her son.

leaders.bio_codex: Tomyris was queen of the Massagetae, a nomadic people of the steppe east of the Caspian Sea and beyond the Araxes, around 530 BCE. Herodotus, writing a century later, says that Cyrus the Great, having taken Babylon, sought to marry her and was refused, bridged the river to invade, and on Croesus's advice left a camp stocked with wine as a trap. The Massagetae under her son Spargapises took the camp, drank, and were captured; Spargapises killed himself. Tomyris then met Cyrus in the hardest battle, Herodotus says, that barbarians ever fought, and the Persians were destroyed and Cyrus killed. She filled a skin with human blood and put his head in it. Other ancient writers give Cyrus other deaths, and no Persian record describes his end. The Massagetae left kurgans, horse burials and gold across the steppe, but no writing, and Tomyris survives only in the history of her enemies' enemies.
leaders.legacy: She is the queen who, in the only account that survives, killed the greatest king of her age for the death of her son.

leaders.name: Trajan

personality.temperament: The Senate voted him the title Optimus, the best, and for a thousand years prayed that each new emperor be luckier than Augustus and better than Trajan. He was the first emperor born outside Italy, a career soldier adopted by an old man who needed the army's loyalty. He marched with his men, founded a welfare fund for poor children, built a harbour, a forum, a market and a column, and took the empire to its largest extent. He was fond of wine and of boys and the historians note both without heat.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Optimus Princeps, likes leaders who expand and dislikes those with small empires; Rome under him reached its widest borders.

leaders.bio_codex: Marcus Ulpius Traianus was born in 53 CE at Italica in Spain, the son of a consul, and commanded legions on the Rhine and the Danube. Nerva adopted him in 97 to secure the army and died in January 98; Trajan took the throne without entering Rome for a year. He fought two wars against Decebalus of Dacia, in 101 to 102 and 105 to 106, destroying the kingdom and taking its gold mines, and told the story in the spiral relief of his column. He annexed Nabataea in 106. He spent the Dacian treasure on the Forum of Trajan, Trajan's Market, the baths on the Esquiline, the harbour at Portus and roads and bridges across the provinces, and he set up the alimenta to feed poor children in Italy. In 113 he went east, took Armenia and in 116 marched down the Tigris to the Persian Gulf, the only Roman to see it. Revolts behind him forced a withdrawal; he died at Selinus in Cilicia in August 117. Hadrian, named heir on the deathbed, gave the east back.
leaders.legacy: He took Rome to its greatest size and built so well in the capital that the Senate called him the best of all princes.

leaders.name: Victoria
leaders.polity: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland; the British Empire
titles: Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

personality.temperament: She was eighteen and five feet tall when they woke her to tell her she was queen, and she asked to be left alone for an hour. She married her cousin Albert, bore nine children, and when he died at forty-two wore black for the remaining forty years. She disliked Gladstone and adored Disraeli, who made her an empress. She wrote two thousand five hundred words a day in her journal and most of Europe's royal houses descend from her. She reigned longer than any British monarch before her and the age took her name.
personality.agenda_tie: Her agenda, Sun Never Sets, likes leaders who settle on her continent and dislikes those who keep her from new ones; the empire covered a quarter of the land.

leaders.bio_codex: Alexandrina Victoria was born at Kensington Palace in 1819 and succeeded her uncle William IV on 20 June 1837, the last of the Hanoverians in Britain. She married Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg in 1840 and governed with him, through the Chartists, the Irish famine, the Great Exhibition of 1851 and the Crimean War, until his death in December 1861. She withdrew from public life for a decade and the republican press grew; Disraeli drew her out and had her proclaimed Empress of India in 1876. Her reign saw the vote extended three times, the railways built, the Indian Mutiny and the Crown's assumption of India, the scramble for Africa and the Boer War. Her Golden and Diamond Jubilees in 1887 and 1897 were the empire's own festivals. She died at Osborne on 22 January 1901 at eighty-one, having reigned sixty-three years, with her grandson the German Kaiser at her bedside.
leaders.legacy: She reigned for sixty-three years over a quarter of the world and lent her name to the age.

leaders.name: Wilfrid Laurier
titles: Knight Grand Cross of St Michael and St George

personality.temperament: He called it the sunny way, the policy of persuasion over coercion, and he used it for fifteen years to hold a country of two languages and two faiths together through a school crisis, a South African war and a naval bill. He was the first French Canadian prime minister and the first to be knighted. He said the twentieth century would belong to Canada and filled the prairies to make it true. He lost power over free trade with the United States and died still leading the opposition.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, The Last Best West, likes leaders who settle tundra and dislikes those who ignore it; he settled the prairies with a million immigrants.

leaders.bio_codex: Henri-Charles-Wilfrid Laurier was born at Saint-Lin, Canada East, in 1841, trained in law at McGill, and entered the Commons in 1874. He led the Liberal Party from 1887, won the 1896 election on the Manitoba Schools question, and governed for fifteen years, the longest unbroken term in Canadian history. His immigration minister Clifford Sifton opened the prairies to two million settlers from Britain, the United States and eastern Europe; Alberta and Saskatchewan became provinces in 1905; the Grand Trunk Pacific was begun; the wheat economy was built. He sent volunteers, not conscripts, to the Boer War, created a Canadian navy in 1910 that satisfied neither the imperialists nor the Quebec nationalists, and in 1911 lost the election over reciprocity, a free trade treaty with Washington. He opposed conscription in 1917 and held Quebec for the Liberals while losing the rest. He died in Ottawa in February 1919 and fifty thousand people followed the coffin.
leaders.legacy: He governed Canada for fifteen years by persuasion, filled the West, and said the century would be Canada's.

leaders.name: Yongle
leaders.faith: Chinese state religion; patron of Buddhism and Taoism

personality.temperament: He took the throne from his nephew in a three-year civil war and had the scholar who refused to write the accession edict executed with his family to the tenth degree, nine hundred people. He then moved the capital to Beijing and built the Forbidden City, sent Zheng He's treasure fleets to Africa, commissioned an encyclopaedia of eleven thousand volumes, invaded Vietnam and led five campaigns into Mongolia in person. He died on the last one. The Ming kept his capital and burned his fleet.
personality.agenda_tie: His agenda, Treasure Fleet, likes leaders whose trade routes bring him gold and dislikes those who send none; the fleets sailed to collect tribute.

leaders.bio_codex: Zhu Di was the fourth son of the Hongwu Emperor, founder of the Ming, and was made Prince of Yan at Beijing to hold the northern frontier against the Mongols. When his father died in 1398 the throne passed to a grandson, the Jianwen Emperor, who began to strip the princes of their power. Zhu Di rebelled in 1399 and in 1402 took Nanjing; his nephew vanished in the palace fire. He took the reign name Yongle, perpetual happiness, and purged the court. From 1406 he built the Forbidden City and in 1421 moved the capital to Beijing, reopened the Grand Canal to feed it, and raised the Porcelain Tower at Nanjing. He sent the eunuch admiral Zheng He on six voyages with fleets of three hundred ships to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa. He annexed Vietnam in 1407, commissioned the Yongle Encyclopaedia, and led five expeditions into the steppe, dying on the return from the last in August 1424. His grandson ended the voyages.
leaders.legacy: He seized the throne, built Beijing, and sent the largest fleet the world had seen to Africa; his heirs kept the city and sank the fleet.
